headline: Vermont engineers to drill Wrightsville Dam above Montpelier this week
dek: The three-week study will examine the 115-foot flood-control dam, its foundation and an auxiliary spillway as the state weighs future safety work.
body: Vermont dam engineers are scheduled to begin drilling at Wrightsville Dam above Montpelier on Monday, Oct. 5, starting a three-week examination of the structure, the soil beneath it and the bedrock around its auxiliary spillway. The work is expected to continue through about Oct. 23, according to a [Vermont Daily Chronicle report](https://vermontdailychronicle.com/dam-protecting-montpelier-2-on-safety-priority-list-drilling-starts-oct-5/) citing the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation.

Wrightsville is a 115-foot earthen dam on the North Branch of the Winooski River in Middlesex. It holds back a reservoir upstream from Montpelier and was built in the 1930s as part of a flood-control system created after the devastating 1927 flood. A Vermont Agency of Natural Resources presentation to lawmakers lists the dam at 1,525 feet long, with storage capacity of about 36,000 acre-feet, and identifies flood control, recreation and hydropower among its purposes. The [state Dam Safety Program](https://dec.vermont.gov/water-investment/dam-safety) says its mission is to reduce risks to life, property and the environment from dam incidents and failures.

The drilling is an assessment, not a repair project. The Chronicle reported that crews will take samples from inside the earthen embankment, from underlying soils and from the rock near the auxiliary spillway. Vermont officials expect the work to reduce uncertainty around seepage, internal erosion and slope-stability questions. The state’s project materials, as summarized in the [Vermont Legislature’s dam-safety presentation](https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2024/WorkGroups/House%20Corrections%20and%20Institutions/Bills/H.882/Witness%20Documents/W~Eric%20Blatt~Capital%20Budget%20Adjustment%20-%20Agency%20of%20Natural%20Resources%20-%20Drinking%20Water%20State%20Revolving%20Fund%20and%20Dam%20Safety~2-14-2024.pdf), describe this kind of assessment as a way to fill engineering data gaps before officials choose a rehabilitation, removal or other risk-reduction option.

Wrightsville ranks second on Vermont’s risk-priority list for 18 state-owned dams with high or significant hazard potential, behind East Barre Dam, according to the state materials and the current report. That ranking does not mean the dam is the second most likely in Vermont to fail. It combines the ways a structure could be vulnerable with the potential consequences downstream, including the presence of Montpelier below Wrightsville. The state’s high-hazard label likewise describes the possible consequences of a failure, not a declaration that the dam is currently unsafe.

That distinction matters because Wrightsville has continued to serve as a flood-control asset. During the July 2023 floods, water in the reservoir rose close to the auxiliary spillway and Montpelier officials warned that more water could add to flooding along the North Branch. An independent [Bridge report](https://thebridgevt.org/2023/08/wrightsville-dam-performed-as-designed-officials-say-but-whats-next/) said state and Army Corps inspectors found the dam satisfactory in a post-flood inspection and reported no new deficiencies. The episode nevertheless exposed how quickly an extreme storm can narrow the margin between routine reservoir operations and emergency concern.

A separate study with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is examining whether the reservoir could be operated differently during and after major storms. Options described in the current reporting include adding a gate or gate system, changing conditions downstream and revising the reservoir’s operating manual. That work addresses a different question from the drilling: how to release stored water more flexibly during back-to-back storms. Neither study is a final repair decision.

During the drilling, the state expects reservoir levels and river flows to remain unchanged and says the dam will retain its flood-control function. Vehicles are expected to occupy one lane of Horn of the Moon Road across the dam, with traffic control in place for roughly three weeks. Reservoir users should expect construction noise, while officials say no closure is planned. The state expects the drilling study to be completed in December, after which the findings can inform the next engineering and funding decisions.

For Montpelier and communities along the North Branch, the immediate takeaway is that the state is gathering information before committing to a permanent intervention. The dam’s priority ranking reflects the consequences of a possible failure and the limits of available safety funding, not a new emergency declaration. Residents seeking official updates should use Vermont DEC and local emergency-alert channels while the work proceeds.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Vermont to drill Wrightsville Dam above Montpelier
seoDescription: Vermont engineers will drill Wrightsville Dam above Montpelier from Oct. 5 to Oct. 23 to study the dam, its foundation and spillway.
sourceName: Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, as reported by Vermont Daily Chronicle
